Joe Hill wrote it in 1911 for his song "The Preacher and the Slave" to weaponize humor against a major frustration of the labor movement.
At the time, street preachers from organizations like the Salvation Army (whom the Wobblies mockingly nicknamed the "Starvation Army") would set up right next to union rallies.
They would play loud brass instruments to drown out the labor organizers, preaching to starving, overworked laborers that they shouldn't worry about their miserable working conditions, low wages, or hunger on Earth, because if they were good, obedient citizens, they would get their glorious reward in heaven.
Hill found this theology incredibly manipulative-a way to pacify desperate workers so they wouldn't strike. So, he hijacked one of their favorite church hymns ("In the Sweet By-and-By") and rewrote the lyrics to mock them:
“Long-haired preachers come out every night,
Try to tell you what's wrong and what's right;
But when asked about something to eat
They will answer with voices so sweet:
You will eat, by and by,
In that glorious land above the sky;
Work and pray, live on hay,
You'll get pie in the sky when you die."
The background of pie in the sky

So simple and reproducible
I see why these became anthems

Before his tragic end,Joel spent years working as a brilliant cartoonist and songwriter for the *Wobblies*, where he famously coined the enduring idiom *“Pie in the sky”* -an empty promise of a future reward- in his satirical song  "*The Preacher and the Slave*".

Decades later, Baez seamlessly recontextualized this traditional union ballad into a contemporary anti-war statement by performing it while heavily pregnant and dedicating it to her husband, David Harris,who was federally imprisoned for resisting the Vietnam War draft,ultimately cementing the song's message of an omnipresent movement for justice spanning "from *San Diego* up to *Maine*” . ‎<This message was edited>

The Richat Structure, famously known as the Eye of the Sahara, is a massive, circular geological feature in the Adrar Plateau of Mauritania. Spanning nearly 40 kilometers in diameter, it consists of concentric rings of igneous and sedimentary rock that have been exposed through millions of years of erosion. Originally thought to be an asteroid impact crater due to its perfect circularity, scientists now classify it as a deeply eroded geologic dome that was pushed up by magma but never erupted. Within the complex landscape of psychosomatic medicine, a highly debated and controversial condition involves individuals who report experiencing debilitating physical symptoms whenever they believe they are in close proximity to everyday environmental stressors. Sufferers report a wide array of non-specific, multi-system issues, including chronic headaches, severe fatigue, skin tingling, dizziness, and sleep disturbances.
However, decades of rigorous, double-blind provocation studies—where participants are exposed to real environmental triggers versus sham (fake) signals without their knowledge—have consistently shown that sufferers are unable to accurately detect when the actual stressors are active. Because of this lack of a biophysical mechanism, mainstream medical organizations, including the World Health Organization, do not recognize it as a legitimate medical diagnosis, often classifying it under the broader umbrella of Idiopathic Environmental Intolerance.
Instead, extensive research suggests that the severe physical distress is driven entirely by a powerful nocebo effect. Serving as the dark mirror image of the well-known placebo effect, the nocebo effect is a psychological and physiological phenomenon where a person's negative expectations, anxiety, or mere anticipation of harm actively manifest as real, distressing bodily symptoms. In the case of this specific condition, the deep-seated belief that a nearby object is emitting a hazardous, invisible force triggers a genuine cascade of stress hormones, causing the body to experience authentic physical suffering born entirely from a perceived threat.
Identify this controversial medical condition

Q: While X is today a member of the EU, there was significant initial hesitation and intense political debate, specifically because of X's legal commitment to "perpetual neutrality". Enshrined in its 1955 Constitution as the price for ending the post-WWII Allied and Soviet occupation, neutrality prohibited X from joining military alliances or hosting foreign military bases. This stance indirectly influenced X’s path to the EU and required a major reinterpretation of what its neutrality actually meant, and it was due to this same stance that X was actually a part of the EFTA from 1960 to 1995, since the EFTA was (and is still) seen as an alternative collective for countries that countries that want to retain some kind of neutrality while still being part of a European collective. ID X

Q: Austria's reinterpretation of its neutrality vis-a-vis the EU, actually was significantly influenced by X's own history in these regards. X was also part of the EFTA, from 1960 to 1973, after which it joined the European Economic Community (EEC), which was the EU's precursor. Unlike with Austria, while neutrality did not cause significant hesitancy when X first joined the EEC in 1973, it became a massive source of public anxiety and political gridlock during later decades as it expanded. As the EEC transitioned from a trade bloc into a political union, the policy neutrality in X faced serious domestic legal challenges, including interventions by its Supreme Court. To solve this issue, this island country's government had to secure legally binding guarantees from Brussels. The EU formally declared that nothing in the treaties could affect X's military neutrality or force it into a collective defense pact. ID X

Calcio (Italian) — literally "a kick"; named after Calcio Fiorentino, the violent Renaissance ball game played in Florence's piazzas. The one famous non-cognate that quizzers might get.
Labdarúgás (Hungarian) — labda (ball) + rúgás (kicking); a pure native calque, "ball-kicking." Hungarian borrows almost nothing here.
Nogomet (Croatian/Slovenian) — noga (foot/leg) + met (throw/cast); a deliberate 19th-century Slavic coinage to avoid the loanword, used in Croatia and Slovenia while Serbia/Bosnia use fudbal.
Jalkapallo (Finnish) — jalka (foot) + pallo (ball); native Finnish calque, no borrowing.
Kopaná / Fotbal — Czech historically used kopaná (from kopat, "to kick") as the native term alongside the loanword.
Voetbal (Dutch) — voet + bal; a true native compound rather than a phonetic loan, even though it's transparent.
Zúqiú / 足球 (Mandarin) — zú (foot) + qiú (ball); the East Asian calque, shared into Japanese/Korean.
Bóng đá (Vietnamese) — bóng (ball) + đá (to kick); native compound, word order reversed ("ball-kick").
Piłka nożna (Polish) — piłka (ball) + nożna (of-the-foot); a native two-word phrase rather than a loan.
Knattspyrna (Icelandic) — knöttur (ball) + spyrna (a kick); Iceland's characteristic purist coinage, deliberately archaic-sounding.

The US military however, has officially embraced the track by incorporating it into the repertoires of its elite musical touring units. The 'Six-String Soldiers', a premier acoustic country and bluegrass group of the official U.S. Army Band (Pershing's Own), actively performs the song. The modern U.S. military can use the song without institutional friction because the U.S. Armed Forces transitioned to an all-volunteer military in 1973. Because the draft basically no longer exists, the song's biting critique of conscription is viewed by the military as a historical artifact of the Vietnam-era, rather than a protest against today's active-duty forces. candidates.text: Q.	Around 550 million years ago in Ediacaran to early Cambrian times, long before complex life crawled onto land, a shallow sea lay across what is now northern A and slowly baked dry under an arid sun. As it evaporated, it left behind a thick basal sheet of crystalline halite, laced with potash and gypsum, that geologists now call the B Range Formation. For the next 500 million years, this layer simply waited, buried and forgotten. Then, about 50 million years ago, the northbound C plate plowed into D. That collision did not create this B the way it created marine limestone on the high peaks, it merely pried these ancient evaporite beds loose and shoved them southward and upward along thrust faults, so that a seabed older than the dinosaurs ended up riding piggyback on a young mountain wall. The B Range rises abruptly from the flat A plains and runs about 200 km along the southern edge of the Pothohar Plateau, from the Jhelum River westward to the Sindhu near Kalabagh. Legend holds that it was found by accident in the late 4th century BCE, when the sick horses of E’s cavalry started licking the rocks, and they recovered soon after. Whatever the truth of that tale, the B was traded in Mughal markets as far as Central Asia, fought over by the Sikhs, and finally industrialized under the British, whose engineer H. Warth introduced the “room and pillar” method here in 1872. The Khewra B mine is now the world's second-largest B mine, a tourist spectacle of glowing chambers, B-brick mosques, and miniature monuments carved from B. B from this region is known as F G B, with F being a geographic indicator and G being a color, although the B Range is at least 100 km away from the nearest F. ID A, B, C, D, E, F, and G.
